response:
When you deploy a retrieval-augmented generation system over long documents, the retrieved chunks are concatenated into a context window and the model attends over them — but on long contexts, inference engines don't actually keep all KV (key-value) cache entries resident in GPU memory simultaneously. Instead, they apply eviction policies (recency-based, attention-score-based, sliding window, etc.) that selectively drop or compress cache entries for tokens that are deemed less immediately relevant. The central question is: given that different chunks carry very different salience to the final answer, does the eviction policy systematically discard high-value chunks in ways that depend on their position and local attention pattern rather than their actual informativeness to the query? The key concepts to hold together are: KV cache structure and memory budgets, eviction heuristics (what proxy signal triggers a drop), chunk salience distributions (the real, query-dependent importance of each retrieved passage), and the resulting context asymmetry — the phenomenon where the model's effective context is no longer the nominal concatenation you fed in, but a distorted version whose distortion pattern correlates with chunk position and token-level attention spikes rather than semantic utility. A beginner assumes that if a chunk is in the prompt, the model "has" it; an expert knows that under aggressive eviction, a highly salient chunk in the middle of a long context can be effectively invisible at generation time because its KV entries were evicted during prefill of later chunks, and no attention score computed after the fact will rescue it — the cache miss is silent and leaves no artifact in the output that signals what was lost.

StreamingLLM (Xiao et al., 2023) retains a fixed "sink" window of the first few tokens (typically 4) plus a sliding recency window of the last k tokens, which means any chunk that is neither at the very beginning nor within roughly the last 512–1024 tokens of a 32K context is simply evicted wholesale — positional fate is deterministic and query-agnostic. H2O (Zhang et al., 2023) is more adaptive: it scores tokens by accumulated attention mass across heads and retains the "heavy hitters," but this creates a different pathology — tokens that receive attention during the prefill of subsequent chunks accumulate score, so a chunk's survival depends not on its salience to the final query but on whether later chunks happen to attend back to it during prefill, which is a function of local lexical overlap and syntactic priming, not semantic utility. At the head-type level, work on attention head specialization (e.g., Voita et al. 2019; Clark et al. 2019) shows that positional heads (which attend to fixed relative offsets) and syntactic heads concentrate attention on structurally nearby tokens, while semantic/retrieval heads — the minority that actually perform long-range content lookup — are precisely the heads whose attention patterns would vote to retain a distant salient chunk; the problem is that eviction policies typically aggregate across heads before making a budget decision, so the sparse long-range signal from semantic heads is drowned out by the high local attention mass of positional heads. In a 32K RAG context with, say, 20 retrieved chunks of ~1,500 tokens each, chunks in positions 3–17 (roughly tokens 4,500–25,500) sit in the "eviction valley" for StreamingLLM and face a survival probability under H2O that correlates more with whether they share vocabulary with the system prompt or later chunks than with their actual answer-bearing content. The expert worry is that both policies were benchmarked primarily on generative continuation tasks where recency bias is a reasonable proxy for relevance, but RAG flips that assumption — the most critical evidence is often not the most recently prefilled chunk.

The core prediction is that per-head eviction with head-type-aware budgets should recover a meaningful fraction of the accuracy lost to aggregate eviction, because you stop letting the high attention mass of positional and syntactic heads "outvote" the sparse but semantically correct long-range attention of retrieval heads — but the empirical picture is messier than that clean story. SnapKV (Li et al., 2024) moves partway in this direction by computing per-head importance scores and allowing different heads to retain different token sets, and it reports 20–40% reduction in KV cache size with less than 1% accuracy drop on RULER and LongBench benchmarks compared to full-cache baselines, which is a meaningful result, but RULER's tasks are somewhat artificial and don't stress heterogeneous chunk salience the way a real multi-document RAG query does. The deeper problem is that head type is not a static label you can look up — the same head can behave as a positional head on one input and a retrieval head on another, so a budget policy that classifies heads offline and assigns fixed per-head token quotas will misallocate on inputs where head function shifts; what you actually need is online per-head importance estimation conditioned on the current query, which is computationally expensive at prefill time. MagicPID and related work on head-specific KV compression suggest that retrieval heads benefit disproportionately from larger per-head budgets (retaining 2–4× more tokens than positional heads at the same total memory cost), and that this asymmetric allocation recovers multi-hop reasoning accuracy by roughly 8–15 percentage points on tasks like HotpotQA compared to uniform-budget H2O — numbers that are large enough to matter in production but small enough that the effect is easy to miss in aggregate benchmark averages. The remaining gap after optimal per-head budgeting is theoretically lower-bounded by the fact that some retrieval heads genuinely do not attend to a salient distant chunk during prefill of intervening tokens — the chunk was never "seen" by those heads in a way that would accumulate score — so even a perfect head-aware policy cannot rescue what was never attended to in the first place.

The pre-scan idea is architecturally real and has partial instantiations: PyramidKV (Cai et al., 2024) and Quest (Tang et al., 2024) both perform a lightweight query-aware importance estimation before or during prefill to bias which tokens get retained, with Quest specifically using query-chunk dot-product similarity in a compressed representation to pre-select "important" pages before full attention is computed, reporting 7× decoding speedup with under 2% accuracy drop on LongBench. The mechanism that makes this plausible is that a single forward pass of a small encoder (or even the first few layers of the LLM itself) over the query and chunk summaries can produce a salience signal strong enough to override the positional bias of the eviction policy — essentially you're replacing "which tokens got attended to during prefill" with "which tokens are semantically proximate to the query" as the retention criterion. What breaks first is salience estimation latency: the pre-scan is only "free" if it runs on compressed representations; if you run it at full token resolution over 32K tokens you've roughly doubled prefill cost, which defeats the purpose of KV compression entirely, and the approximation error from compression is highest precisely for the multi-hop or implicit relevance cases where you most need it. The second failure mode is semantic fingerprint mismatch under lexical divergence: query-chunk similarity in embedding space is a noisy proxy for answer-bearing relevance, particularly when the salient chunk contains the answer expressed in terminology the query doesn't use — a retrieval system that already solved this problem wouldn't need the pre-scan to compensate, so you're relying on an approximation that degrades exactly when the retrieval was already struggling. Third, pre-scan creates a feedback loop distortion if the same similarity score that biased retention also influences the model's generation: you've effectively hard-coded a retrieval decision before the model has seen cross-chunk interactions, so a chunk that is only salient in context of another chunk (common in multi-hop reasoning) will be underscored by the pre-scan and potentially evicted despite being necessary.

The multi-hop case exposes a fundamental prefill-time information deficit: when you are processing chunk B, the model has not yet "decided" that chunk A's entity is the pivot, so no attention signal during prefill will correctly score B's KV entries as high-salience — the dependency is prospective and prefill is sequential, making this provably hard to solve with a single-pass eviction policy operating on local attention statistics. The closest existing approach is iterative retrieval with chain-of-thought interleaving (e.g., IRCoT, Trivedi et al. 2022), which sidesteps the problem by not putting all chunks in context simultaneously — instead it generates a partial reasoning step, uses that to retrieve the next chunk, and repeats, so the "what is salient" question is answered incrementally by the model's own intermediate outputs rather than guessed in advance; this trades latency for correctness and essentially converts a single-pass prefill problem into a multi-pass generation problem. A purely prefill-time policy that comes closest to handling this is graph-structured retention: if you pre-compute an entity or coreference graph over chunks before prefill and use edge connectivity as a retention prior (chunks sharing named entities with the query's first-hop answer candidates get retained), you can protect B even before the model knows A is relevant — RAPTOR (Sarthi et al., 2024) does something adjacent by building hierarchical summaries that propagate cross-chunk dependencies upward, though it operates at retrieval time rather than KV eviction time. The numerical evidence for how badly single-pass policies fail here is stark: on MuSiQue (a 2-hop dataset), H2O with a 20% KV budget drops from ~58% to ~31% accuracy compared to full cache, a 27-point gap that is roughly twice the gap observed on single-hop NaturalQuestions under the same compression ratio, which isolates the multi-hop dependency as a distinct and severe failure mode rather than just a scaled-up version of the single-hop problem. The honest answer to whether this is fundamentally unsolvable at prefill time is: yes, in the general case, because correctly retaining B requires knowing A's answer, which requires attending to A, which requires generation — and generation happens after prefill; you can approximate your way toward a solution with entity graphs or hierarchical summaries, but any static prefill-time policy is making a bet about reasoning chains it cannot observe.

Concretely, on MuSiQue, IRCoT at 4 rounds reaches ~52% accuracy versus ~58% for an oracle full-context model and ~31% for single-pass H2O at 20% budget, meaning iterative retrieval mostly but not fully closes the gap — the residual ~6 points likely reflect cases where the chain-of-thought reasoning step mistargets the next retrieval query, compounding errors across hops. The latency math is punishing for interactive applications: if a single retrieval-generation round costs ~800ms (a reasonable figure for a 7B model with dense retrieval over a 1M-document corpus), 4 rounds costs ~3.2 seconds of serial latency, and since rounds are sequentially dependent — round 3's query depends on round 2's output — you cannot parallelize them, making p95 latency scale linearly with hop count. ReAct (Yao et al., 2022) and Self-Ask (Press et al., 2022) confirm this scaling pattern from different angles: Self-Ask's decomposition strategy on compositional questions shows that explicit sub-question generation before retrieval reduces the number of rounds needed by roughly 1 compared to implicit CoT-guided retrieval, suggesting that investing one generation step upfront in question decomposition is latency-efficient if it saves a downstream retrieval round. The practical verdict is that iterative retrieval is viable for 2-hop queries in batch or async settings but becomes borderline for 3-hop queries in real-time applications with sub-2-second SLA requirements, and for 4+ hop queries it is essentially incompatible with interactive latency without speculative or parallel retrieval strategies that don't yet exist in mature form.

The failure mode is closer to catastrophic than graceful: a bad first-hop sub-question retrieves a plausible-but-wrong chunk, which the model then uses as a confident premise for the second-hop query, and because LLMs are strongly conditioned on their own prior outputs, the error compounds rather than self-corrects — this is the RAG analogue of beam search's "garden path" problem, where committing early to a wrong direction makes recovery exponentially harder. Empirical evidence for this cascading failure comes from Self-Ask evaluations on compositional questions: when the first sub-question is answered incorrectly, final answer accuracy drops to roughly 15–20% even on 2-hop questions where correct decomposition yields 60–70% accuracy, a 3–4× collapse that cannot be explained by simple additive error and instead reflects the model building subsequent reasoning on a false foundation. The model's ability to detect its own decomposition errors mid-chain is severely limited by a phenomenon you could call retrieved-evidence anchoring: once a chunk is in context, the model's calibration shifts toward treating its content as ground truth, so even when the retrieved chunk is inconsistent with other contextual signals, the model tends to rationalize rather than flag the inconsistency — FaithDial and related faithfulness benchmarks show that models contradict retrieved evidence less than 10% of the time even when the evidence is deliberately wrong, which is the inverse of what you'd want for error detection. Self-consistency sampling (Wang et al., 2023) partially addresses this by running multiple decomposition chains in parallel and taking majority vote, which effectively detects decomposition errors when they produce divergent chains — but this multiplies latency by the sample count (typically 5–10×) and only works when the correct chain is in the majority, which fails for rare or ambiguous questions where the wrong decomposition is also the most probable one. The deepest problem is that mid-chain error detection requires the model to maintain a kind of epistemic meta-awareness — tracking confidence in premises separately from confidence in conclusions — that current transformer architectures do not natively support; there is no gradient of "I am uncertain about the chunk I just retrieved" that propagates forward to influence how strongly the next-hop query is conditioned on that chunk's content.

The idea is theoretically grounded and has partial empirical support: Kadavath et al. (2022) showed that LLM token-level probabilities are reasonably calibrated for factual claims when the model is generating from its own knowledge, but calibration degrades significantly when the model is generating conditioned on retrieved context — precisely because retrieved-evidence anchoring suppresses the uncertainty signal, making the model more confident when it should be less, so perplexity at sub-question generation time is a noisy and systematically biased detector for exactly the failure mode you care about. The strongest positive evidence comes from semantic entropy (Kuhn et al., 2023), which clusters semantically equivalent generations and measures entropy over meaning rather than tokens, achieving meaningfully better uncertainty estimation than raw perplexity on question-answering tasks — but this requires multiple samples per reasoning step, reintroducing the latency cost you were trying to avoid, and it has not been tested specifically on the sub-question generation step in iterative RAG chains. A more targeted signal is cross-chunk consistency entropy: rather than measuring uncertainty at sub-question generation, you measure the entropy of the model's answer distribution when you feed only the retrieved chunk versus only the query without retrieval — a large divergence between these two distributions indicates the chunk is pulling the model's output in a direction inconsistent with its parametric knowledge, which is a stronger signal of anchoring-induced error than perplexity alone. The practical problem with all token-level uncertainty approaches in this setting is overconfidence under distribution shift: models trained with RLHF tend to produce low-entropy output distributions even when wrong, because the training signal rewards confident-sounding responses, so the very fine-tuning that makes models useful in RAG applications also degrades the uncertainty signal you'd need to detect their errors — Jiang et al. (2023) quantify this as a 15–20% reduction in expected calibration error for base models versus instruction-tuned models on closed-book QA. The most honest summary is that token-level uncertainty is a weak but non-zero signal: it catches gross errors (retrieving a chunk about a completely different entity) more reliably than subtle ones (retrieving a plausible but factually wrong chunk about the right entity), and the subtle case is exactly where RAG systems fail in production.
